title: Persistent Vitamin B12 Hypervitaminemia: Identification of Biomarkers for the Early Detection of Solid Cancers
official: Hypervitaminémie B12 Persistante : Identification de Biomarqueurs Pour le dépistage précoce Des Cancers Solides-KB12
summary:
Elevated blood levels of vitamin B12 are sometimes discovered unexpectedly during routine blood tests. Persistently elevated vitamin B12 levels can occur for several reasons, including liver disease, kidney disease, blood disorders, vitamin B12 supplementation, and certain solid cancers. However, a high vitamin B12 level alone does not indicate whether cancer is present, and it remains unclear which patients should undergo further investigations.

The KB12 study aims to determine whether measuring specific blood markers involved in vitamin B12 transport and uptake can help distinguish elevated vitamin B12 levels associated with solid cancers from those related to other conditions. Researchers hypothesize that these markers may differ according to the underlying cause of the elevated vitamin B12.

In this multicenter study, participants with persistently elevated vitamin B12 levels will provide a blood sample for laboratory analysis. Researchers will compare the levels of these markers between participants with solid cancers and those with other identified causes of elevated vitamin B12. Participants will also be contacted by telephone approximately one year later to check for any newly diagnosed conditions. Participation will not change their usual medical care.

The results may help develop more targeted approaches to investigating persistently elevated vitamin B12 levels, with the long-term goal of improving early cancer detection while avoiding unnecessary examinations.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Age ≥18 years.
* Affiliation to a French social security system.
* Persistent hypercobalaminemia, defined as total serum vitamin B12 \>1,000 ng/L on at least two measurements performed at least 4 weeks apart.
* A single identified cause of persistent hypercobalaminemia among the following:

  * Myeloid malignancy, diagnosed according to current international classifications (WHO 2022 and/or International Consensus Classification 2022).
  * Chronic liver disease with cirrhosis, established according to current international recommendations using non-invasive biological and imaging assessments, with histological confirmation if necessary.
  * Severe chronic kidney disease, defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate \<30 mL/min/1.73 m² persisting for more than 3 months.
  * Excessive exogenous vitamin B12 supplementation, defined as intramuscular administration ≥1,000 µg/month and/or oral supplementation ≥3,000 µg/week, in the absence of pernicious anemia.
  * Histologically confirmed invasive solid cancer, with at least locally advanced disease (local extension or regional lymph node involvement).
* Written informed consent.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Presence of multiple concurrent causes of hypercobalaminemia, or insufficient clinical data to exclude an additional underlying cause.
* Pregnancy, breastfeeding, or childbirth.
* Deprivation of liberty by judicial or administrative decision.
* Involuntary psychiatric treatment.
* Persons under legal protection.
* Inability to provide informed consent.
